coherence.reasons: Both use the same four-pillar structure (market, unit economics, cash, alternative) under a clear 'do not launch' governing thought. X is more consistent: it measures contribution after store costs throughout, so the claim that every observed case loses money is carried by the figures (-$12.6, -$6.2, -$1.8 against the plan's +$2.02), and the governing thought's reopening condition is picked up by the gates slide. Y's unit-economics pillar says Parcelbird Now 'would lose money per order', but its headline figure and comparison table use contribution before store costs, where the best site shows +$0.5. Y's slide 11 title ('Only Zipcart-style fees make a median order pay') also sits awkwardly beside that pillar. Y's fourth pillar is honestly qualified ('if sales outgrow today's pipeline') and well supported.

judgment.reasons: Both reach the key's preferred conclusion (decline, fund the software) and both reject a one-store pilot with numbers. Y weighs the alternatives more fully against the board's stated objectives. It designs the strongest version of the pilot (Zipcart fees, stop date, acquisition cost included) and still shows it loses about $0.30M a year at median volume. It also tests whether the recommended software path reaches profitability within current cash: breakeven ARR of $11.0M, about $6.6M used, a 40% growth sensitivity, and the admission that it needs about 72 contracts, twice today's pipeline. X's software case is thinner: late-stage deals cover the hires, and the path to profitability is left as a 'burn plan' to be set. X does give better forward governance, with four quantified gates and a capital-light reopening test using customer-site data. X's pilot is costed at median economics without fees, a weaker version to reject. On balance Y's check that its own recommendation meets the investors' constraint slightly outweighs X's gates.

evidence.reasons: X reproduces every critical calculation in the key: median -$6.17, best-on-every-driver about -$1.80 (key -$1.76), pop-up -$12.6 (key -$12.57), Zipcart fixes at a median site -$1.05 (matches the key), about 6 months of runway, and a full-cost break-even basket of about $63. It adds a one-driver-at-a-time sensitivity of the plan. Y gets -$6.17 and the runway right and adds useful customer maths ($173 per retained customer, $1.53M to fill a store, $27.5M for nine stores). But Y never computes the pop-up or the best site after store costs. Its table labels pre-store-cost figures 'contribution per order', which makes the best site look positive, and its break-even basket ($46.7) and rider speed (3.8) also exclude store costs. Y asserts Zipcart 'kept the same stores and riders', which the pack does not say, shows $3.5M against $3.6M for the same pipeline, and calls $4.77M 'only just' keeping a $4.8M floor. Its software breakeven assumes flat costs while ARR quadruples, though this is disclosed. X's slips are minor: 'demand is still accelerating' and assuming all nine late-stage deals close.

revision.reasons: Both reject the founders' hypothesis while conceding the market-growth point, and both engage with the Zipcart evidence instead of ignoring it or over-reading it. X tests the 'density will fix it' claim more completely. It shows that even the best observed basket and density combined still lose about $1.80 after store costs. It quantifies the Zipcart fix at a median site (-$1.05) and at top-of-range volume (+$0.41), then turns the partial support into an explicit reopening gate of 1,042 orders a day at customer sites. That is the limited, capital-light updating the key describes. Y gives Zipcart a dedicated slide and derives the same break-even volume, and it rightly notes the plan does not use the fee lever. But it leaves the best-site case showing a positive pre-store-cost contribution, never showing that best observed density still loses after store costs, and its reopen test is one line in next steps.

overall.reasons: Both documents would lead the board to the right decision with defensible reasoning. X serves the board somewhat better on the core question of whether the operator economics can work. Its unit economics are complete and fully costed across the pop-up, the median, the best case and the plan. It quantifies the Zipcart counter-evidence correctly, and it gives the board measurable gates for reopening the question without spending runway. Y's distinctive strength is a real path-to-profitability model for the software alternative and a better-designed pilot option. But its pre-store-cost framing weakens the central unit-economics argument and leaves out two of the key's critical figures (pop-up and best case after store costs).
